case.limits: It construes one state statute. It travels only as far as BIPA's reach and the growing family of statutes modelled on it, and federal courts still filter such claims through Article III standing.
case.holding: A person whose biometric data is collected in violation of BIPA is aggrieved and may sue without alleging any further injury. The statutory violation itself is the harm.
case.case_name: Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entertainment Corp.

live_cases.name: Miller v. Clearview AI "Artificial Intelligence" Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The decision that armed BIPA. Face-recognition and voice-model litigation against AI companies proceeds on Rosenbach's rule that collection without the required notice and consent is actionable per se, which is why Illinois is where biometric AI cases are filed and settled at nine and ten figures.

reading.body:
Rosenbach established that collecting biometric data without required notice and consent violates Illinois law actionably on its own, without proof of separate injury. This ruling transformed BIPA from a narrow state statute into the template for biometric privacy litigation that now drives nine and ten-figure settlements against AI companies.

The holding creates statutory standing. A person needs only show that their biometric data was collected in violation of BIPA's procedures. They do not need to prove identity theft, fraud, emotional distress, or any downstream harm. The violation itself is the compensable injury. This flattens the litigation landscape. It means every unauthorized collection event is a distinct claim, and class actions aggregate to substantial sums.

BIPA's reach is narrow by design. It applies only in Illinois and to statutes modelled on it. Federal courts still require Article III standing, which limits some BIPA claims' passage into federal litigation. Yet the doctrine has proven durable. Face-recognition and voice-model companies now face ongoing suits under Rosenbach's rule in the jurisdictions that adopted it. The data does not capture settlement patterns or the cost structure these lawsuits impose on AI development. It shows only the legal rule that made those costs possible.
